source_name: The State of Developer Ecosystem 2025: Coding in the Age of AI, New Productivity Metrics, and Changing Realities
methodology_type: Self-report attitude survey: an online questionnaire of developers reporting their own AI usage, sentiment, and concerns. It is not instrumented/behavioral telemetry, so any 'we review our AI code carefully' response is a stated claim, not an observed action -- exactly the attitude-vs-action gap this research set is tracking.
sample_size: 24,534 developers across 194 countries, surveyed April-June 2025, with geographic, employment, programming-language, and product-use balancing applied to the sample.
pct_distrust_ai_code: No single 'percent who distrust AI code' figure is published, but the survey's top concern about AI is the 'inconsistent/quality of AI-generated code' at 23% of respondents naming it their #1 concern, followed by AI's 'limited understanding of complex code and logic' (18%), privacy/security (13%), negative effect on developer skills (11%), and lack of context awareness (10%). Together these code-quality-adjacent concerns (23% + 18% + 10% = 51%) indicate roughly half of respondents flag code-correctness-related worries as a top concern, even though 85% say they use AI regularly and 62% rely on at least one AI coding assistant/agent/editor day to day.
pct_always_verify: No explicit 'percent who always verify before committing' metric was located in the publicly available report and summary pages. [uncertain]
stated_behavioral_gap: Cannot be precisely computed without a published 'always verify' figure, but the qualitative gap is stark: the same population that names code quality as its top AI concern (23%) and reports privacy/security and context-awareness worries also reports 85% regular AI use and 41% of respondents' own code as AI-generated, with no correspondingly high figure for rigorous checking. The report's own framing calls this out as a 'productivity-verification trade-off': developers use AI extensively while knowing the output needs review, because reviewing AI output is still perceived as faster than writing from scratch. [uncertain]
verification_behavior_detail: The report distinguishes 'checking' effort by experience level rather than giving one aggregate figure: less-experienced developers report that reviewing AI-generated code takes greater effort than their most-experienced peers report. Less-experienced developers also estimate about 45% of their committed code is AI-assisted, versus about 40% estimated by their most-experienced peers. No figure is given for time spent per review, nor whether checking means running tests, reading line by line, or using static analysis tooling.
seniority_breakdown: Experience level shapes both usage and framing of AI, not just verification effort. Less experienced developers estimate a higher share of their own committed code is AI-assisted (about 45%) than the most experienced developers do (about 40%), and less-experienced developers report AI-code review taking more effort than their senior peers report. The two groups also frame AI's role differently: more experienced developers are more likely to describe AI as a 'junior colleague', a content generator, or assign it no defined role, while less experienced developers are more likely to describe AI in a 'teacher' role.
culture_incentive_angle: The report frames developers' relationship to AI as driven by a felt trade-off between speed and control rather than by an explicit blame/career-risk mechanism: fears center on 'losing control' while developers 'care deeply about code quality, reliability, and security' and about preserving their professional sense of competence. No explicit statement about career risk, blame allocation for AI-introduced bugs, or deadline pressure as a named driver was found in the available material. [uncertain]
measured_proxy_angle: The report introduces its own alternative to velocity-style metrics rather than endorsing one: it is subtitled around 'new productivity metrics' and highlights time-saved figures (many AI-using developers report saving more than one hour per week, with a subset saving eight hours or more per week) as a headline productivity signal, alongside sentiment metrics. It does not explicitly name PR throughput, lines-shipped, or feature-count as metrics that leadership optimizes for at the expense of verification, though the emphasis on hours-saved as the headline number is itself a velocity-flavored proxy rather than a quality or defect-rate metric. [uncertain]
human_factors_parallel: Not present in the source material reviewed. [uncertain]
leadership_implication: The report frames a coming shift in job expectations rather than a specific process recommendation: 68% of developers anticipate that AI proficiency will become a job requirement. Beyond this, no explicit instruction to managers (e.g. 'build in review time' or 'stop measuring velocity') was found in the material available. [uncertain]
methodological_caveat: No documented correction, walk-back, or contested-methodology flag was found for this specific edition. The survey does apply sampling balancing (geography, employment, language, product use) as a stated control, and as a self-report instrument its figures on 'review effort' and 'AI-generated code share' are developers' own estimates rather than measured/instrumented values, which is a standing limitation of the format rather than a specific admitted error.
